**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 10, 2026
**Re:** Nipusk Bulk Shipping, Inc. / Lusen Maritime Software LLC: TideRoute Software License Agreement: issues review and negotiating priorities

---

## 1. Executive Summary

Nipusk faces an urgent problem. Its non-renewal letter dated October 20, 2026 was sent **18 days after the October 2, 2026 deadline** in Section 12.2 of the Software License Agreement (the **"SLA"**). On the SLA's terms, Lusen can claim that the SLA renewed automatically for a **three-year Renewal Term through December 31, 2029**, with a **7% fee increase**.

The letter relies on the term sheet's 30-day notice period. That argument is weak, for two reasons:

- the term sheet's renewal provisions were expressly non-binding; and
- the SLA states that it **supersedes the Term Sheet** (SLA Sections 1.3 and 17.4).

The renewal problem is made worse by three other SLA provisions that go beyond the October 2023 term sheet:

1. **Exclusivity (Section 3.4).** Nipusk cannot even procure a replacement product during the Term.
2. **Governing law (Schedule 2, paragraph 9).** Any dispute over Vessel Data, including data return on exit, is moved to English law and London LMAA arbitration.
3. **Assignment (Section 16.3).** Lusen can assign the SLA and its Vessel Data rights to a competing shipowner without consent or notice.

**Our core recommendation** is that Nipusk:

- preserves its written objection to renewal;
- does not take steps that could be treated as repudiation or as acceptance of renewal; and
- opens a commercial negotiation with Lusen promptly, before December 31, 2026, for one of two outcomes:
  - a consensual exit or a short (e.g., one-year) renewal; or
  - if Nipusk stays, an amendment that conforms the SLA to the term sheet on all five points below.

### Summary table

| # | Issue | Location | Severity | Recommended fix (short form) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Late non-renewal notice | D3 (Oct. 20, 2026 letter), ¶¶1–2, read with SLA §§12.1, 12.2, 17.2 | **Critical / urgent** | Reserve rights; negotiate exit or a 1-year renewal before Dec. 31, 2026 |
| 2 | Automatic 3-year renewal, 90-day notice | SLA §12.2 (with Sch. 1 ¶5) | High | Amend to 1-year renewals and 30-day notice; cap or remove the 7% uplift |
| 3 | Overbroad exclusivity | SLA §3.4, read with §1.1 "Competing Product" and "Vessel" | High | Narrow to voyage-optimization software on Nipusk-owned dry-bulk vessels |
| 4 | English law / LMAA arbitration for Vessel Data | SLA Sch. 2 ¶9, read with §§1.3, 15.1 | High | Delete ¶9 or conform it to Delaware law and Wilmington courts |
| 5 | Unrestricted assignment by Lusen | SLA §16.3, read with §16.2 and §1.1 "Permitted Transferee" | Medium–High | Require consent; exclude competitors; give Nipusk a termination and data-deletion right |

---

## 2. Documents Reviewed

| Ref | Document | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Software License Agreement, effective January 1, 2024, with Schedules 1 (Commercial Terms), 2 (Vessel Data Terms) and 3 (Service Levels) | Operative contract. The signature blocks and notice addresses in our copy are **blank** (see Section 5). |
| D2 | Term Sheet dated October 16, 2023 | Non-binding except §§11–13 (§1.2). Signature blocks are blank. |
| D3 | Nipusk non-renewal letter dated October 20, 2026 (courier and email) | Relies on Term Sheet §5.2. |
| D4 | Lusen draft Schedule 3 (Service Levels), Draft 1, November 15, 2023 | Superseded prior draft marked "subject to contract". It does not affect the analysis (see Section 4). |

### Key framework provisions

These provisions apply to every issue below:

- **Order of precedence and supersession (SLA §1.3).** If the main body and a Schedule conflict, "the Schedule prevails over the main body." "This Agreement supersedes the Term Sheet."
- **Entire agreement (SLA §17.4).** This clause repeats that the SLA, including its Schedules, is the entire agreement and supersedes the Term Sheet.
- **Effect of these provisions.** The term sheet cannot be used to cut back the SLA's terms. Where the SLA departs from the term sheet, the fix must be a **written amendment signed by both parties** (§17.3).

---

## 3. Issue-by-Issue Analysis

### Issue 1: The non-renewal notice was late, so Lusen can claim the SLA renewed through December 31, 2029

**Where it appears**

- D3, Nipusk's letter dated October 20, 2026, ¶1.2 (notice of non-renewal) and ¶2 (basis of notice).
- Read with SLA §12.1 (Initial Term ends December 31, 2026), §12.2 (notice must be given at least 90 days before term end) and §17.2 (notice is effective on receipt).

**What happened**

- **Deadline.** The Initial Term ends December 31, 2026 (§12.1). Section 12.2 requires written notice of non-renewal "at least ninety (90) days before the end of the then-current term." The last day for notice was therefore **October 2, 2026**.
- **Nipusk's letter.** The letter is dated October 20, 2026 and was sent by courier and email. Under §17.2, notice is effective only **on receipt**, so the effective date is October 20, 2026 at the earliest and probably later. That is at least **18 days late**.
- **How the letter justifies itself.** ¶2.1 relies expressly on Term Sheet §5.2 (30 days' notice). It does not claim compliance with SLA §12.2.

**Why it matters for Nipusk**

- **Three more years of fees.** On the SLA's terms, the SLA renews automatically on January 1, 2027 for a three-year Renewal Term ending **December 31, 2029**. Under Schedule 1 ¶5, the per-Vessel fee rises 7%, from US$18,500 to **US$19,795** per Vessel per year, for the whole Renewal Term. Fees are invoiced annually in advance (Sch. 1 ¶3), so Lusen will likely invoice the 2027 contract-year fee on or around January 1, 2027.
- **The term sheet argument is weak.**
  - Term Sheet §1.2 provides that the term sheet is not binding except §§11–13. The renewal provision (§5) is not one of the binding sections.
  - SLA §§1.3 and 17.4 provide that the SLA supersedes the Term Sheet.
  - A Delaware court is likely to apply §12.2 as written.
  - We should not advise the client that the October 20 letter was effective to end the SLA on December 31, 2026.
- **The exposure is uncapped.** Under §11.5, the §11.4 liability cap and the §11.3 exclusion do **not** apply to "Licensee's obligation to pay the Fees." If Nipusk walks away and Lusen sues for three years of renewal fees, the claim is not limited by the cap.
- **Exclusivity runs on.** If the SLA has renewed, the §3.4 exclusivity covenant (Issue 3) continues through 2029. Under §3.4, Nipusk also may not "license, procure, develop, deploy" a Competing Product during the Term. Contracting with a replacement vendor now could itself breach the SLA.
- **Data return may be disputed.** The letter's request for return and deletion of Vessel Data (¶3.2) assumes the SLA expires on December 31, 2026. Lusen is likely to resist it. Any dispute about it may fall under Schedule 2 ¶9 (English law and LMAA arbitration; Issue 4).
- **The letter has useful features.** It clearly states that Nipusk "does not wish to renew." It reserves all rights (¶4.1). It states that continued use or payment before December 31, 2026 is not agreement to renewal (¶4.2). Nothing in the folder shows that Nipusk has accepted the renewal.

**Recommended course of action**

1. **Do not concede, but do not rely on the term sheet argument.** Keep the written objection on record. Avoid any statement that the SLA has renewed. Avoid any act that could look like affirming the renewal, such as signing renewal paperwork or paying a renewal invoice without a reservation of rights.
2. **Do not repudiate.** Nipusk should not stop using the system or refuse invoices outright after December 31, 2026 without advice. If it does, it risks an uncapped fee claim and a breach-of-exclusivity claim.
3. **Open a commercial negotiation now, before December 31, 2026.** Possible asks, in order of preference:
   - (a) a consensual termination effective December 31, 2026, possibly with a short paid transition period;
   - (b) a single **one-year** renewal at the existing fee (no 7% uplift), with a 30-day notice period, consistent with the term sheet;
   - (c) if Lusen insists on the renewal, an amendment package covering Issues 2–5.

   Points of leverage include:
   - the gap between the term sheet and the SLA, which can be used as a fairness and relationship point;
   - Lusen's interest in keeping a reference customer; and
   - the possibility of adding Vessels.
4. **Assess fallback arguments, but treat them as secondary.** We should consider whether there is any basis for reformation, for example mutual mistake about the renewal terms or knowledge on Lusen's part of a unilateral mistake. We should also consider waiver or estoppel arising from Lusen's conduct since October 2. These depend on facts we do not yet have (see Section 5). On the current record, I would not expect them to succeed.
5. **Check whether Lusen has responded.** The letter asked Lusen to confirm data-return arrangements by **November 6, 2026**, and that date has passed. Any Lusen response, or a failure to respond, shapes our next step.
6. **Diarize.** The next relevant dates are the expected January 1, 2027 invoice and, if the renewal stands, the deadline for non-renewal notice for the Renewal Term: **October 2, 2029** (90 days before December 31, 2029).

---

### Issue 2: Automatic renewal for successive three-year terms with 90 days' notice (term sheet: one-year terms, 30 days)

**Where it appears**

- SLA §12.2 (Renewal).
- Read with Schedule 1 ¶5 (7% Renewal Fee Adjustment) and §§1.3 and 17.4 (supersession).
- Compare Term Sheet §5.2.

**What it says**

- Section 12.2 provides that the SLA "shall renew automatically for successive three-year Renewal Terms" unless either party gives written notice of non-renewal "at least ninety (90) days before the end of the then-current term." The sentence requiring 90 days' notice appears twice in §12.2.
- Schedule 1 ¶5 raises the per-Vessel fee by 7% at the start of each Renewal Term.
- Term Sheet §5.2 provided for **one-year** renewal terms and **30 days'** notice.
- Term Sheet §5.3 left renewal fees to the definitive agreement. It did not agree to a 7% escalator.

**Why it matters for Nipusk**

- **Longer lock-in.** Each missed deadline commits Nipusk to three years, not one, at compounding increases of 7% per Renewal Term.
- **Earlier deadline.** The notice window opens 60 days earlier than the commercial deal contemplated. That is the trap that caused Issue 1.
- **Supersession.** Because §§1.3 and 17.4 make the SLA supersede the Term Sheet, Nipusk is bound by §12.2 as written. The term sheet does not cure it.
- **Interaction with other clauses.** The clause works together with the exclusivity covenant (Issue 3) and the uncapped fee obligation (§11.5), which makes the lock-in more serious.

**Recommended fix**

Amend §12.2 and Schedule 1 ¶5, either as part of the Issue 1 negotiation or in any continuing relationship:

- renewal terms of **one year**;
- non-renewal notice of **30 days** before term end, consistent with Term Sheet §5.2;
- delete the 7% uplift or replace it with a capped index-linked adjustment (e.g., the lower of CPI and 3%), payable only if notified at least 60 days before renewal;
- add a Lusen obligation to send a **reminder notice** 30–60 days before each notice deadline (a modest protective ask);
- remove the duplicated sentence in §12.2.

Separately, I recommend that the client diarize all contractual notice deadlines in a central contract register.

---

### Issue 3: Overbroad exclusivity covenant

**Where it appears**

- SLA §3.4 (Exclusivity).
- Read with the §1.1 definitions of "**Competing Product**," "**Vessel**" and "**Affiliate**," and §1.3 (supersession).
- Compare Term Sheet §7.

**What it says**

- **The covenant.** Under §3.4, Nipusk "shall not, and shall procure that its Affiliates do not, license, procure, develop, deploy or use any Competing Product on or in respect of any Vessel." Nipusk must also use TideRoute "as its sole solution" for all Competing Product functions "across all Vessels."
- **"Competing Product" (§1.1)** covers:
  - (a) fleet management;
  - (b) voyage optimization, weather routing and speed and consumption planning;
  - (c) emissions monitoring and reporting, including CII, EEXI, EU ETS, FuelEU Maritime and IMO DCS;
  - (d) hull, propeller and engine performance monitoring; and
  - (e) crew management, crew planning and crew scheduling.

  The definition applies whether the product is licensed from a third party, developed internally or provided as a subscription service.
- **"Vessel" (§1.1)** means any vessel "owned, chartered, managed or operated by Licensee or any Affiliate of Licensee, wherever located in the world."
- **Term Sheet §7.1** limited exclusivity to "voyage-optimization software only, for dry-bulk vessels owned by Nipusk." Term Sheet §7.2 confirmed that Nipusk was free to use other providers "for all other functions and vessels."

**Why it matters for Nipusk**

- **More functions are covered.** The covenant covers five categories of software. TideRoute does not offer some of them at all: under Schedule 1 there is **no crew-management module** and no EEXI or FuelEU Maritime functionality listed. Read literally, Nipusk is barred from using *any* crew-management or FuelEU compliance tool, including tools it builds in-house.
- **More vessels are covered.** The covenant reaches chartered-in, managed and operated tonnage, and all Affiliates, worldwide. Charterers and managers often require their own platforms on vessels they charter or manage. Nipusk or its Affiliates may already be in breach.
- **The effect is anti-competitive and has regulatory implications.** Emissions compliance is a fast-moving regulatory area (EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime). Being tied to one vendor's tools across the whole fleet is a real operational and compliance risk.
- **Exit is harder.** "Procure" and "develop" mean that Nipusk cannot line up a successor vendor during the Term. This is critical if the SLA has renewed (Issue 1).
- **No cure from the term sheet.** Under §1.3 the SLA supersedes the Term Sheet, so the narrower agreed scope does not apply.

**Recommended fix**

Amend §3.4 and the definitions to match Term Sheet §7:

- limit exclusivity to **voyage-optimization functions** only (item (b) of the "Competing Product" definition);
- limit it to **dry-bulk vessels owned by Nipusk** and onboarded under Schedule 1. Delete "chartered, managed or operated" and the Affiliate extension for this purpose;
- delete "procure" and "develop", or carve out evaluation, procurement and implementation of a successor product during the last 12 months of any term or after notice of non-renewal or termination;
- carve out software required by charterers, pools, managers, flag or class, or by law;
- add an express statement that Nipusk is free to use other providers for all other functions and vessels, mirroring Term Sheet §7.2.

**Action point:** Ask the client what other fleet, emissions, performance and crew software Nipusk and its Affiliates currently use, so we can assess its existing breach exposure (see Section 5).

---

### Issue 4: English law and London LMAA arbitration for Vessel Data disputes, which override the Delaware choice

**Where it appears**

- SLA Schedule 2 (Vessel Data Terms), ¶9 (Law and Disputes).
- Read with §1.3 (Schedules prevail), §15.1 (Delaware law, Wilmington courts) and Schedule 2 ¶1 (definition of Vessel Data).
- Compare Term Sheet §13.

**What it says**

- **SLA §15.1** chooses Delaware law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in Wilmington, Delaware.
- **Schedule 2 ¶9** provides that Schedule 2 "and any dispute or claim arising out of or in connection with Vessel Data" is governed by "the laws of England and Wales." It refers any such dispute to arbitration in London under the terms of the "London Maritime Arbitrators Association" before a tribunal of three arbitrators.
- **"Vessel Data" (Schedule 2 ¶1)** is defined very broadly. It covers:
  - AIS position data;
  - noon reports;
  - fuel and bunkering data;
  - route, speed and weather data;
  - engine and hull performance data;
  - emissions data;
  - cargo and charter-party particulars; and
  - all reports and outputs derived from any of them.
- **§1.3** provides that a Schedule prevails over the main body if they conflict.
- **Term Sheet §13** chose Delaware law and Wilmington courts for the term sheet *and the Definitive Agreement*. It is one of the binding sections under Term Sheet §1.2. However, it is likely to be treated as superseded by the SLA (§§1.3 and 17.4).

**Why it matters for Nipusk**

- **English law and LMAA arbitration control Vessel Data disputes.** Because of §1.3, ¶9 prevails over §15.1. It is therefore **not correct** to say that all disputes under the SLA are governed by Delaware law. Disputes arising out of or in connection with Vessel Data are governed by English law and go to LMAA arbitration.
- **Most operational disputes are likely to be caught.** The software's whole function is to process Vessel Data, so "in connection with" is likely to capture most operational disputes. Examples include data security incidents (Sch. 2 ¶¶5–6), misuse of data or aggregated data (¶4), routing or performance output failures, and **data return and deletion on exit** (¶8). That last category is immediately relevant to Issue 1.
- **Disputes may be split between two forums.** A dispute over renewal or fees would probably go to Delaware. A connected dispute over data return would go to London. This means:
  - duplicated cost;
  - possible inconsistent outcomes;
  - arguments over which forum has jurisdiction; and
  - an opportunity for Lusen to choose the forum that suits it.
- **The agreed choice is displaced.** This departs from the agreed Delaware choice (Term Sheet §13). Nipusk is likely to have negotiated on the basis of Delaware.

**Recommended fix**

- **Delete Schedule 2 ¶9** or conform it to §15.1, so that Delaware law and Wilmington courts apply to all disputes, including Vessel Data disputes.
- Amend §1.3 so that §15 (Governing Law and Disputes) prevails over any Schedule. More generally, the main body should prevail on legal boilerplate, and the Schedules should prevail only on their operational subject matter.
- **In the interim:** before any dispute over data return arises, we should advise the client that ¶9 may apply. Any proceedings strategy should account for both forums. The §15.2 escalation process applies before starting proceedings, and §15.3 preserves urgent injunctive relief.
- **Optional:** if the client's commercial team prefers maritime arbitration, a single LMAA clause covering *all* disputes is better than the current split. Delaware is the agreed position, however, and should be the opening ask.

---

### Issue 5: Lusen may assign the SLA, and its Vessel Data rights, to anyone, including a competing shipowner, without consent or notice

**Where it appears**

- SLA §16.3 (Assignment by Licensor).
- Read with §16.2 (mutual consent requirement "except as permitted in Section 16.3") and the §1.1 definition of "**Permitted Transferee**."
- Compare Term Sheet §10.3.

**What it says**

- **§16.2** requires each party's prior written consent to any assignment, "except as permitted in Section 16.3."
- **§16.3** allows Lusen to assign, transfer or novate the SLA, in whole or in part, "together with its rights in and to Vessel Data under Schedule 2, to any Permitted Transferee without the consent of or notice to Licensee."
- **"Permitted Transferee" (§1.1)** means "any person, **including any shipowner, ship operator or charterer**," that acquires all or any part of Lusen's business or assets, and any Lusen Affiliate.
- **Nipusk has no equivalent right.**
- **Term Sheet §10.3** agreed that neither party may assign without the other's prior written consent.

**Why it matters for Nipusk**

- **A competitor could end up holding Nipusk's data.** A competing dry-bulk owner or charterer could buy any part of Lusen's business, even a minor asset, and take over the SLA together with Lusen's licence over Nipusk's Vessel Data. That data includes route, fuel, performance, cargo and charter-party particulars, which are highly sensitive commercially.
- **Nipusk would not know.** Because no notice is required, Nipusk might not learn that the assignment had happened.
- **There is no exit right.** No termination right is triggered by an assignment or change of control. Nipusk would remain locked in, potentially through 2029 (Issues 1 and 2), and bound by exclusivity (Issue 3), with a counterparty it never chose.
- **Partial assignment creates uncertainty.** Lusen can assign "in part", so different obligations could end up with different entities. That makes it unclear who is responsible for support, service levels and data security.
- **Remaining protections are limited.** The confidentiality obligations (§10) and the Schedule 2 restrictions would bind the assignee. Enforcing them against a competitor after the fact is, however, a poor substitute for preventing the transfer.

**Recommended fix**

Amend §16.3 and the definition of "Permitted Transferee" to:

- require **Nipusk's prior written consent** to any assignment by Lusen, consistent with Term Sheet §10.3. At a minimum, consent should not be unreasonably withheld, with a carve-out only for a solvent sale of **all or substantially all** of Lusen's business to a non-competitor;
- **exclude** any shipowner, ship operator, charterer, pool or their Affiliates from "Permitted Transferee", and delete "or any part";
- require **advance written notice** (e.g., 30 days) of any permitted assignment or change of control of Lusen;
- give Nipusk a right to **terminate without liability**, with a refund of prepaid Fees, if Lusen assigns or undergoes a change of control. Include a right to require return and deletion of Vessel Data at that point;
- prohibit any assignment of Vessel Data rights separately from the SLA as a whole, and confirm that the assignee's use of Vessel Data stays limited to the Schedule 2 ¶3 purpose;
- optionally, give Nipusk a reciprocal right to assign to its Affiliates or to the purchaser of its fleet.

---

## 4. Prior Draft Service Level Schedule (D4): No Issue Identified

The November 15, 2023 draft Schedule 3 (D4) is marked "Draft for Discussion," "Subject to contract. Not for execution," and "Draft 1."

- **Superseded.** It has no contractual effect. The executed SLA contains its own Schedule 3, and §17.4 makes the SLA the entire agreement.
- **Same commercial terms.** I compared it with executed Schedule 3. The core commercial terms are the same: 99.5% availability, the severity matrix, the service credit bands with a 20% cap, the 30-day claim period, and chronic-failure termination at 98% in three months of any rolling twelve.
- **Protections dropped from the draft.** The draft contained a few process protections that are **not** in the executed Schedule 3:
  - retention of monitoring records for 12 months (D4 ¶2.2);
  - reasonable efforts to avoid interrupting routing outputs for Vessels at sea during maintenance (¶3.3);
  - updates on Severity 1 incidents every two hours (¶5.2); and
  - quarterly service reviews (¶8.2).

These omissions are minor. If the SLA continues, they are reasonable "asks" for the amendment package. They do not affect the analysis above.

**Possible leverage point:** if the client has records of availability below 98% in any three months of a rolling twelve-month period, the chronic-failure right in executed Schedule 3 ¶7 could offer an exit route independent of Issue 1. The notice must be given within 60 days after the third qualifying month. We need Lusen's monthly service reports (Sch. 3 ¶8) to check this.

---

## 5. Gaps in the Folder and Information Needed from the Client

Please obtain the following before we finalize advice:

1. **Executed SLA.** Our copy has blank signature blocks and blank notice addresses. We need the signed version to confirm that the terms reviewed are the executed terms and to identify Lusen's address for notices under §17.2.
2. **Proof of delivery of the October 20 letter.** We need courier tracking and the email delivery record, to confirm the date of receipt (notice is effective on receipt, §17.2). We should also confirm whether any earlier written notice or email about non-renewal was sent before October 2, 2026.
3. **Lusen's response, if any.** The letter asked for confirmation by November 6, 2026. We need any reply, invoice, renewal notice or other communication since October 2026.
4. **Negotiation history.** We need correspondence and redlines between the term sheet (October 2023) and signing. In particular, did Nipusk see and accept the changes to §§3.4, 12.2, 16.3 and Schedule 2 ¶9? This affects any reformation or mistake argument and our negotiating narrative.
5. **Signed term sheet.** Our copy of the term sheet is unsigned. We need to know whether it was countersigned.
6. **Fleet and fees.** We need:
   - the current number of Vessels on TideRoute (Schedule 1 ¶2) and the annual fees paid;
   - the dates of invoices; and
   - whether any Vessels were added under Schedule 1 ¶2.

   This lets us quantify the renewal exposure, which is three years of fees with a 7% uplift.
7. **Other software in use.** We need a list of fleet-management, emissions-reporting, performance-monitoring and crew-management tools used by Nipusk and its Affiliates on any owned, chartered-in or managed vessel. This lets us assess existing exposure under §3.4.
8. **Replacement vendor plans.** Has Nipusk signed or begun procuring a successor platform? This is relevant to the "procure" limb of §3.4.
9. **Service performance.** We need Lusen's monthly service reports for 2025–2026, to test the chronic-failure termination right (Sch. 3 ¶7).
10. **Commercial objectives.** We need to know the client's preference: a full exit on December 31, 2026, a short extension, or continuing with renegotiated terms. We also need to know how much fee exposure it would accept to settle.

---

## 6. Recommended Next Steps

1. **This week.** Collect the items in Section 5, especially the executed SLA, proof of delivery and any Lusen response. Confirm the client's commercial objective.
2. **Within about two weeks.** Send a without-prejudice letter or hold a call with Lusen under the §15.2 executive escalation process. Propose a consensual exit on December 31, 2026 or a one-year renewal at current fees. The written reservation of rights stays in place.
3. **In parallel.** Prepare an amendment covering Issues 2–5, together with the minor Schedule 3 points from D4. This will be the price of any continuing relationship.
4. **Before January 1, 2027.**
   - Agree how any renewal invoice will be handled. If payment becomes necessary to avoid breach, it should be made under an express reservation of rights.
   - Instruct the client not to procure or deploy any Competing Product until the exclusivity position is resolved.
5. **Ongoing.** Set up a contract-deadline register. If the renewal stands, the next non-renewal deadline is October 2, 2029.

Please let me know if you would like me to draft the letter to Lusen or the amendment.

## 3. Issue-by-Issue Analysis

### Issue 1: Late non-renewal notice and likely automatic renewal (URGENT)

**Where it appears:** The Letter, paragraphs 1.2 and 2.1–2.2, read with Agreement Sections 12.1, 12.2 and 17.2 and Schedule 1, paragraph 5.

**What the documents say:**
- Section 12.1 fixes the end of the Initial Term at December 31, 2026.
- Section 12.2 requires written non-renewal notice at least 90 days before the end of the then-current term. Counting back 90 days from December 31, 2026 gives a deadline of **October 2, 2026**.
- The Letter is dated October 20, 2026, which is **18 days after the deadline**. It states that Nipusk "does not wish to renew". It relies expressly on the Term Sheet's 30-day notice period (Term Sheet §5.2), and it reserves Nipusk's rights (§4).
- Under Section 17.2, a notice is effective only on receipt. Receipt must therefore have been on or after October 20, so the notice is late on any view.

**Why it matters for Nipusk:**
- On the Agreement's terms, Lusen can say the Agreement renewed automatically on January 1, 2027 for a **three-year Renewal Term through December 31, 2029**.
- The per-Vessel fee would rise 7% to US$19,795 for the whole Renewal Term (Schedule 1, ¶5).
- Fees are invoiced annually in advance (Schedule 1, ¶3), so Nipusk could face a full-year invoice on January 1, 2027.
- The liability cap (§11.4) does not limit Nipusk's obligation to pay Fees (§11.5).
- The Term Sheet argument is weak. Section 1.3 and Section 17.4 both state that the Agreement supersedes the Term Sheet, and Section 17.4 is an entire-agreement clause. The renewal provisions of the Term Sheet were also non-binding (Term Sheet §1.2).
- I have not identified any provision in the Agreement that gives Nipusk a unilateral right to end the Renewal Term early. The only exits are:
  - termination for uncured material breach (§12.3);
  - insolvency (§12.4);
  - chronic SLA failure (Schedule 3, ¶7);
  - terminating a non-conforming module (§9.2).
- The Letter is helpful in one respect. It is a clear, contemporaneous objection and it reserves rights, so Nipusk has not acquiesced in renewal. Paragraph 4.2 also says that continued use and payment before December 31, 2026 is not agreement to renewal.

**Recommended course of action:**
1. **Do not concede that the Agreement has renewed, and do not withdraw the Letter.** Further correspondence should be sent "without prejudice to the Letter". It should restate Nipusk's objection and reservation of rights.
2. **Approach Lusen promptly to negotiate a consensual outcome**, ideally before Lusen issues its January 1, 2027 invoice. The options, in order of preference, are:
   - (a) a mutually agreed expiry on December 31, 2026, possibly in exchange for a short paid transition period;
   - (b) a one-year renewal on the Term Sheet terms (30-day notice) at the current fee, with no 7% uplift;
   - (c) a renewal with a termination-for-convenience right for Nipusk on short notice.
   Any outcome must be recorded in a written amendment signed by both parties (§17.3).
3. **Use the commercial levers Nipusk has:**
   - Lusen's likely interest in keeping the relationship on agreed terms;
   - the Term Sheet's evidence of what the parties actually agreed;
   - the clean-up points in Issues 2 to 4 below, which Lusen may prefer to concede rather than face a contested renewal.
4. **Review the record for other exit routes:**
   - SLA performance history (chronic failure under Schedule 3, ¶7);
   - any material breaches by Lusen (§12.3);
   - any module non-conformity (§9.2).
5. **Prepare for the January 1, 2027 invoice.** If it arrives before a deal is reached, consider disputing it in good faith in writing before the due date under §5.4. Note that this carries its own dispute risk if the renewal is ultimately upheld. Also see Issue 3 on where any such dispute would be heard.
6. **Plan the transition in parallel.** If Nipusk has a replacement provider lined up, check the commitments it has made and their timing. Nipusk may need to stay on TideRoute for longer than it planned.

### Issue 2: Renewal terms depart from the Term Sheet (three-year renewals, 90-day notice, escalating fees)

**Where it appears:** Agreement Section 12.2, read with Schedule 1, paragraph 5 and Sections 1.3 and 17.4. For comparison, see Term Sheet Section 5.2.

**What the documents say:**
- Section 12.2 provides for automatic renewal "for successive three-year Renewal Terms" unless notice is given "at least ninety (90) days" before the end of the then-current term.
- Schedule 1, paragraph 5 adds a 7% per-Vessel fee increase at the start of each Renewal Term.
- The Term Sheet agreed **one-year** renewal terms with **30 days'** notice (§5.2). It left renewal fees to the Definitive Agreement (§5.3).

**Why it matters for Nipusk:**
- Each missed window locks Nipusk in for three more years rather than one.
- The 90-day window is three times longer than agreed, so it is easier to miss. That is exactly what has happened here.
- The 7% uplift compounds with each Renewal Term.
- Because the Agreement supersedes the Term Sheet (§§1.3, 17.4), Nipusk is bound by Section 12.2 as written. It cannot fall back on the Term Sheet terms.

**Recommended fix:**
- Amend Section 12.2 to provide for **one-year** Renewal Terms on **30 days'** written notice, consistent with the Term Sheet.
- Either delete Schedule 1, paragraph 5, or replace it with a modest, capped increase (for example, CPI-linked, not to exceed a stated percentage) that applies only on a one-year renewal.
- Add a Nipusk right to terminate for convenience during any Renewal Term on, say, 90 days' notice.
- As a practical safeguard, ask Lusen to send a renewal reminder notice at least 30 days before each notice deadline.
- Internally, Nipusk should diarize all contract notice deadlines.

### Issue 3: English law and London (LMAA) arbitration for Vessel Data disputes override the Delaware choice

**Where it appears:** Agreement Schedule 2 (Vessel Data Terms), paragraph 9, read with Section 1.3 and Section 15.1. For comparison, see Term Sheet Section 13.

**What the documents say:**
- Section 15.1 selects Delaware law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in Wilmington, Delaware. This matches Term Sheet §13, which the Term Sheet stated would be binding (§1.2).
- Schedule 2, paragraph 9 provides that Schedule 2, "and any dispute or claim arising out of or in connection with Vessel Data", is governed by the **laws of England and Wales**. Such disputes are to be referred to arbitration in London under the terms of the **London Maritime Arbitrators Association**, before three arbitrators.
- "Vessel Data" is defined very broadly (Schedule 2, ¶1). It covers AIS, noon reports, fuel and bunkering data, route, speed, weather, performance and emissions data, charter-party particulars, and all reports and outputs derived from them. In practice, almost everything the Software processes is Vessel Data.
- Section 1.3 provides that a Schedule prevails over the main body in the event of conflict.

**Why it matters for Nipusk:**
- As written, the Delaware choice does **not** govern disputes "arising out of or in connection with Vessel Data". Those disputes go to English law and London arbitration. Given how wide the definition is, these include disputes over:
  - routing outputs;
  - SLA failures affecting data;
  - data security incidents;
  - return and deletion on exit;
  - very possibly Fee disputes that turn on data-driven performance.
- There is a real risk of **parallel proceedings**: the same commercial dispute (including the current renewal dispute, if it touches data return under Schedule 2, ¶8) could be split between the Wilmington courts and a London tribunal, with arguments about which forum has jurisdiction.
- A three-member LMAA tribunal is likely to cost more than the agreed forum. Nipusk would also have to deal with a governing law it did not bargain for.
- This departs from the Delaware law and forum terms that the Term Sheet stated were binding. However, the Agreement's supersession clause (§§1.3, 17.4) makes that point hard to rely on.

**Recommended fix:**
- Delete Schedule 2, paragraph 9, or conform it to Section 15.1 (Delaware law; Wilmington courts).
- Amend Section 1.3 so that Section 15 prevails over any Schedule on governing law and dispute resolution.
- If Lusen insists on arbitration for data matters, as a fallback require a single dispute-resolution regime for all claims under the Agreement, so that disputes cannot be split.
- In the near term, assess the renewal dispute and the data-return request in the Letter (§3.2) with this split forum in mind before any proceedings are started.

### Issue 4: Lusen may assign the Agreement and Vessel Data rights to anyone, including competitors, without consent or notice

**Where it appears:** Agreement Section 16.3, read with Section 16.2 and the Section 1.1 definition of "Permitted Transferee". For comparison, see Term Sheet Section 10.3.

**What the documents say:**
- Section 16.2 requires prior written consent for assignment by either party "except as permitted in Section 16.3".
- Section 16.3 lets Licensor assign, transfer or novate the Agreement, in whole or in part, "together with its rights in and to Vessel Data under Schedule 2, to any Permitted Transferee **without the consent of or notice to Licensee**".
- "Permitted Transferee" (§1.1) means any person, "**including any shipowner, ship operator or charterer**", that acquires all or **any part** of Lusen's business or assets, and any Lusen Affiliate.
- Nipusk has no equivalent right. The Term Sheet agreed mutual consent for any assignment (§10.3).

**Why it matters for Nipusk:**
- Lusen could sell even a small part of its business to a competing dry-bulk owner, operator or charterer. That buyer could take over the Agreement and Lusen's rights to Nipusk's Vessel Data, which includes route, fuel, bunkering, performance and charter-party data. That data is commercially sensitive.
- Nipusk would receive no notice and would have no right to object or terminate. If renewal is upheld, that exposure runs until 2029.
- A partial assignment could also fragment Nipusk's counterparty, with different modules held by different entities.
- The confidentiality protections in Section 10 would pass to the assignee. They would not stop a competitor from gaining access to the data in the first place.

**Recommended fix:**
- Delete Section 16.3, or restrict it so that Lusen may assign without consent only:
  - to a successor to **all or substantially all** of its business;
  - that is **not** a shipowner, operator, charterer or other competitor of Nipusk; and
  - that assumes all of Lusen's obligations in writing.
- Require prior written notice of any assignment.
- Give Nipusk a right to terminate without penalty, with a fee refund and full Vessel Data return and deletion under Schedule 2, ¶8, if the Agreement or the Vessel Data rights pass to a competitor or to a party Nipusk reasonably objects to.
- Prohibit partial assignments.
- Consider making the assignment right mutual, so that Nipusk can assign to an Affiliate or to a successor of its fleet business.
